messages.subject: confidence limits for morphological disparity
parts:
Hello everyone!

I need to calculate confidence limits for morphological disparity. I tried to follow the instructions in this thread and obtain distributions of bootstrapped Procrustes variances via bootstrapping of residuals. For my own data I need to use custom null model for pairwise() comparisons. It seems that I don't understand something and do it all wrong, because I get very strange confidence limits. 
Reproducible example with plethodon data is below. 
Thanks in advance!
Marina

library(geomorph)
data(plethodon) 

Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethodon$land)
gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(Y.gpa, site = plethodon$site, species = plethodon$species)

fit_null <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) + site, data = gdf, iter = 999, print.progress = FALSE)
fit_full <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) + site * species, data = gdf, iter = 999, print.progress = FALSE)

gp <- interaction(plethodon$site, plethodon$species)

PW <- pairwise(fit.full, fit.null, groups = gp, covariate = log(gdf$Csize))
SMR <- summary(PW, test.type = "var")
(md <- SMR$vars[, 1])

N <- length(plethodon$species)
Ftt <- fitted(fit_null)
Res <- residuals(fit_null)
vars <- NULL
set.seed(302354)
for(i in 1:999) {
  # 1) resample residuals with replacement (by rows)
  New_res <- Res[sample(N, replace = TRUE)]
  # 2) add these to fitted values, 
  New_obs <- arrayspecs(Ftt + New_res, ncol(Ftt)/2, 2)
  # 3) re-obtain model result (iter = 1) and get disparity
  New_fit_full <- procD.lm(New_obs ~ log(Csize) + site * species, data = gdf, iter = 1, print.progress = FALSE)
  pw <- pairwise(New_fit_full, fit_null, groups = gp)
  smr <- summary(pw, test.type = "var", iter = 1)$vars[, 1, drop = F]
  vars <- cbind(vars, smr)
}
# confidence limits
(cl <- apply(vars, 1, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975)))

Hi Marina,

I believe there are several issues you are encountering.  

First, I don’t think you want to bootstrap residuals from the null model.  This seems to attempt to combine the philosophy of a permutation test and bootstrapping confidence intervals for the estimation of variances.

Second, I think you want to resample within groups, not across all values.  Below is an update to your function that allows this.  (Note also it is not necessary to redo the pairwise test step.)

# Function to bootstrap residuals within groups
sample.win.gp <- function(Res, gp) {
  gp.res <- as.list(by(Res, gp, function(x) x)) # separate Res by groups
  ind <- lapply(gpn, function(x) sample(seq_len(x), replace = TRUE)) # sampling frame
  gp.boot <- lapply(1:length(ind), function(j) gp.res[[j]][ind[[j]], ]) # bootstrap within gp levels
  gp.boot <- do.call(rbind, gp.boot) # put back into matrix
  gp.boot <- gp.boot[order(gp), ] # order as original
  gp.boot
}

for(i in 1:999) {
  New_res <- sample.win.gp(Res, gp)
  gdf$New_obs <- Ftt + New_res
New_fit_full <- procD.lm(New_obs ~ log(Csize) + site * species,

data = gdf, iter = 0, print.progress = FALSE)
  d2.i <- rowSums(resid(New_fit_full)^2)
  smr <- by(d2.i, gp, mean)

vars <- cbind(vars, smr)
}

# confidence limits
(cl <- apply(vars, 1, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975)))

Third, one could argue that because you have size in your model, bootstrapping should make sure to also match the size and shape of specimens.  This would require using the same sampling frame for bootstrapping observed data and Csize, and refitting the model to obtain residuals.  That is a different algorithm, but an easy one to implement.  In the New_res step within the loop, substituted Res with a concatenated (cbinded) matrix of fit_full$LM$Y and Csize, separate them, and update the data frame; e.g.,

bootstrapped <- sample.win.gp(cbind(gdf$Csize, fit_full$LM$Y, gp)
gdf2 <- gdf
gdf2$New_obs <- bootstrapped[, -1]
gdf$Csize <- bootstarpped[,1]
New_fit_full <- procD.lm(New_obs ~ log(Csize) + site * species,

data = gdf2, iter = 0, print.progress = FALSE)

Doing this will make sure that size and shape match.  I recommend doing this if allometry is important to preserve.

Keep in mind that the confidence limits for estimation and from a permutation test are different things.  The UCL in the pairwise summary is the upper confidence limit of the sampling distribution for a test statistic, not confidence limits around the estimation of the descriptive statistic.  The former is a limit in a statistical test where one would change their opinion to “significant”, based on a null model used to generate random test statistics.  The latter defines the precision of the estimation of the descriptive statistic.  Descriptive and test statistics can be the same thing but the respective distributions are not the same, nor are their expected values based on different resampling schemes.

Hope this helps!
Mike

Dear Marina,

I apologize for misleading you.  I tried to offer some tips that should work, generally, but there seems to be a sorting problem.  Rather than try to diagnose and fix that, I came up with a case-specific solution for you.  This example emphasizes how challenging bootstrapping is, as every scenario offers unique considerations.  I checked this time to make sure the results made sense, and they seem to, with some caveats.  First the code:

library(geomorph)
data(plethodon) 

Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethodon$land)
gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(Y.gpa, site = plethodon$site, species = plethodon$species)

fit_null <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) + site, data = gdf, iter = 999, print.progress = FALSE)
fit_full <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) + site * species, data = gdf, iter = 999, print.progress = FALSE)

gp <- interaction(plethodon$site, plethodon$species)
PW <- pairwise(fit_full, fit_null, groups = gp, covariate = log(gdf$Csize))

SMR <- summary(PW, test.type = "var")
(md <- SMR$vars[, 1])

N <- length(plethodon$species)

Ftt <- fitted(fit_full)
Res <- residuals(fit_full)
vars <- md
set.seed(302354)

# Function to values and calculate variances

bootstrap.this.case.only <- function(fit, Csize, gp) {
  Y <- fit$LM$Y
  Z <- cbind(Csize, Y)
  gp.Z <- as.list(by(Z, gp, function(x) x)) 
  
  ind <- lapply(gp.Z, function(x) sample(seq_len(NROW(x)), replace = TRUE)) # sampling frame
  gp.boot <- lapply(1:length(ind), function(j) gp.Z[[j]][ind[[j]], ]) # bootstrap within gp levels
gp.boot <- do.call(rbind, gp.boot) # put back into matrix

gp <- sort(gp) # make sure groups
  form <-fit$LM$form
  gdf2 <- fit$LM$data
  gdf2$Y <- gp.boot[, -1]
  gdf2$Csize <- gp.boot[, 1]

New_fit_full <- procD.lm(New_obs ~ log(Csize) + site * species, 
                           data = gdf2, iter = 0, print.progress = FALSE)
  d2.i <- rowSums(resid(New_fit_full)^2)
  smr <- by(d2.i, gp, mean)

smr
}


for(i in 1:999) {
  vars <- cbind(vars, 
                bootstrap.this.case.only(fit_full, gdf$Csize, gp))
}

# confidence limits
(cl <- apply(vars, 1, summary))

It is possible for the observed values to be extreme in this case (toward the min or max value rather than the center) and if one wishes to generate confidence intervals like this, the mean or median value should be used rather than the observed, because bias is possible.  I don’t have a good sense of what the distribution of variances should be — this is not typically done as a statistical procedure.  The Central Limit Theorem appears to have worked in part (the distributions are symmetric) but I do not know if we should expect the observed variances to be centralized in these distributions.  But, we did this in a way that preserved group sizes.  What if we did not do that, but adjusted groups based on random outcomes, sampling instead from all specimens?

bootstrap.all <- function(fit, Csize, gp) {
  Y <- fit$LM$Y
  Z <- cbind(Csize, Y)
  boot <- sample(1:NROW(Z), replace = TRUE)
  gp <- gp[boot]
  
  form <-fit$LM$form
  gdf2 <- fit$LM$data
  gdf2$Y <- gp.boot[, -1]
  gdf2$Csize <- gp.boot[, 1]
  New_fit_full <- procD.lm(Y ~ log(Csize) + site * species,

data = gdf2, iter = 0, print.progress = FALSE)
  d2.i <- rowSums(resid(New_fit_full)^2)
  smr <- by(d2.i, gp, mean)

smr
}


for(i in 1:999) {
  vars <- cbind(vars, 
                bootstrap.all(fit_full, gdf$Csize, gp))
}

# confidence limits
(cl <- apply(vars, 1, summary))

> md
  Allo.Jord   Symp.Jord  Allo.Teyah  Symp.Teyah 
0.001870410 0.001830881 0.001654327 0.001511529 

But the conclusions appear to be basically the same.  This is a small sample so large residuals might have some impressive leverage, whether randomly included or excluded.  A better example might be more comforting.  But this would be a common statistical concern (small sample size), regardless of data or statistic recalculated in each permutation

Hopefully something in there is helpful for you.  I cannot emphasize enough that bootstrap strategies are diverse and depend on what you are doing with your model.  (In other cases, bootstrapping residuals might make more sense, as you initially started out, but with shape data, one has to question whether that illogical configurations created need to have their Csize updated.  So these above seem at least less wayward.)

Cheers!
Mike

Hi Marina,

I believe there are several issues you are encountering.  

First, I don’t think you want to bootstrap residuals from the null model.  This seems to attempt to combine the philosophy of a permutation test and bootstrapping confidence intervals for the estimation of variances.

Second, I think you want to resample within groups, not across all values.  Below is an update to your function that allows this.  (Note also it is not necessary to redo the pairwise test step.)

# Function to bootstrap residuals within groups
sample.win.gp <- function(Res, gp) {
  gp.res <- as.list(by(Res, gp, function(x) x)) # separate Res by groups
  ind <- lapply(gpn, function(x) sample(seq_len(x), replace = TRUE)) # sampling frame
  gp.boot <- lapply(1:length(ind), function(j) gp.res[[j]][ind[[j]], ]) # bootstrap within gp levels
  gp.boot <- do.call(rbind, gp.boot) # put back into matrix
  gp.boot <- gp.boot[order(gp), ] # order as original
  gp.boot
}

for(i in 1:999) {
  New_res <- sample.win.gp(Res, gp)
  gdf$New_obs <- Ftt + New_res
  New_fit_full <- procD.lm(New_obs ~ log(Csize) + site * species, 
                           data = gdf, iter = 0, print.progress = FALSE)
  d2.i <- rowSums(resid(New_fit_full)^2)
  smr <- by(d2.i, gp, mean)
  vars <- cbind(vars, smr)
}

# confidence limits
(cl <- apply(vars, 1, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975)))

Third, one could argue that because you have size in your model, bootstrapping should make sure to also match the size and shape of specimens.  This would require using the same sampling frame for bootstrapping observed data and Csize, and refitting the model to obtain residuals.  That is a different algorithm, but an easy one to implement.  In the New_res step within the loop, substituted Res with a concatenated (cbinded) matrix of fit_full$LM$Y and Csize, separate them, and update the data frame; e.g.,

bootstrapped <- sample.win.gp(cbind(gdf$Csize, fit_full$LM$Y, gp)
gdf2 <- gdf
gdf2$New_obs <- bootstrapped[, -1]
gdf$Csize <- bootstarpped[,1]
New_fit_full <- procD.lm(New_obs ~ log(Csize) + site * species, 
                           data = gdf2, iter = 0, print.progress = FALSE)

Doing this will make sure that size and shape match.  I recommend doing this if allometry is important to preserve.

Keep in mind that the confidence limits for estimation and from a permutation test are different things.  The UCL in the pairwise summary is the upper confidence limit of the sampling distribution for a test statistic, not confidence limits around the estimation of the descriptive statistic.  The former is a limit in a statistical test where one would change their opinion to “significant”, based on a null model used to generate random test statistics.  The latter defines the precision of the estimation of the descriptive statistic.  Descriptive and test statistics can be the same thing but the respective distributions are not the same, nor are their expected values based on different resampling schemes.

Hope this helps!
Mike

Marina et al. (Mike, Dean and Antigoni),

To add to both Mike and Dean's point on using (non-parametric) bootstrapping based on empirical resampling to compute confidence intervals.

As mentioned in a couple of the papers/books that Dean mentioned, the "percentile"  based confidence intervals (like Mike calculated) are usually an ok starting point,  but are often problematic for somewhat skewed distributions (of resampled estimates, not raw data),  when the observed estimate is near a boundary (e.g. the observed value is close to the minimum possible value it can take for the data set) and with small within group sample sizes. There are some immediate checks (the boot library can help) and the Bias Corrected and Accelerated CIs (BCa) often can provide an improvement. These problems do occur more often for "variance"/"disparity" and phenotypic integration related statistics in my experience (which makes sense because of both being higher moment statistics that are estimated and also are used bounded by a minimum value, with real estimates sometimes "near" that value).  Like Mike showed in the first example, it is usually most sensible to do the sampling within groups of focus (in the boot library this is done via the strata argument, but it is relatively straightforward to code like Mike showed).

So it pays to take some time and patience to work on this. For the particular data set that Mike showed the example for, things mostly behaved reasonably well. In other situations (see our methods in Haber and Dworkin 2017 in Evolution for some discussion of these issues), things can get a bit bonkers though!

The most robust approach for generating CIs from non parametric bootstrapping (sampling with replacement) is the studentized bootstrap. This has greater computational demands as it requires bootstraps of bootstrap samples (to generate standard errors of each resampled data set to normalize the value we use each iteration). Typically (in my experience) this requires about 200 iterations in the internal resampling, so for a typical "10000" bootstrap iterations, it is really computationally more like 20,000,000 iterations total. Thankfully there are ways of making this more efficient so it still (on a relatively new laptop) will only be on the order of 10-20 minutes to run all these iterations. It can also be parallelized relatively easily in R (with some package dependencies). I keep meaning to write a little add-on set of functions to interact with geomorph/RRPP model objects to do so (I have some working examples just with base R, lm functions not with geomorph). Hopefully (if someone bugs me in the late spring), I can sit down and hammer this out, and send the code to Antigoni, Mike and Dean, or just make a little side package. But, alas no time until at least the end of next semester. But if someone does bug me I will work on it. I keep meaning to, but I keep thinking it is just us who suffers with this.

All the best to all of the morphometrics community, and wishing you all a very happy (Gregorian) new year!

Ian

I believe there are several issues you are encountering.  

First, I don’t think you want to bootstrap residuals from the null model.  This seems to attempt to combine the philosophy of a permutation test and bootstrapping confidence intervals for the estimation of variances.

Second, I think you want to resample within groups, not across all values.  Below is an update to your function that allows this.  (Note also it is not necessary to redo the pairwise test step.)

# Function to bootstrap residuals within groups
sample.win.gp <- function(Res, gp) {
  gp.res <- as.list(by(Res, gp, function(x) x)) # separate Res by groups
  ind <- lapply(gpn, function(x) sample(seq_len(x), replace = TRUE)) # sampling frame
  gp.boot <- lapply(1:length(ind), function(j) gp.res[[j]][ind[[j]], ]) # bootstrap within gp levels
  gp.boot <- do.call(rbind, gp.boot) # put back into matrix
  gp.boot <- gp.boot[order(gp), ] # order as original
  gp.boot
}

for(i in 1:999) {
  New_res <- sample.win.gp(Res, gp)
  gdf$New_obs <- Ftt + New_res
  New_fit_full <- procD.lm(New_obs ~ log(Csize) + site * species, 
                           data = gdf, iter = 0, print.progress = FALSE)
  d2.i <- rowSums(resid(New_fit_full)^2)
  smr <- by(d2.i, gp, mean)
  vars <- cbind(vars, smr)

# confidence limits
(cl <- apply(vars, 1, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975)))

Third, one could argue that because you have size in your model, bootstrapping should make sure to also match the size and shape of specimens.  This would require using the same sampling frame for bootstrapping observed data and Csize, and refitting the model to obtain residuals.  That is a different algorithm, but an easy one to implement.  In the New_res step within the loop, substituted Res with a concatenated (cbinded) matrix of fit_full$LM$Y and Csize, separate them, and update the data frame; e.g.,

gdf2 <- gdf
gdf2$New_obs <- bootstrapped[, -1]
gdf$Csize <- bootstarpped[,1]
New_fit_full <- procD.lm(New_obs ~ log(Csize) + site * species, 
                           data = gdf2, iter = 0, print.progress = FALSE)

Mike

Dear Ian, Mike, Dean and Antigoni,

thank you for great advices! Percentile confidence intervals for my data were indeed very asymmetric. Thanks to your help, I was able to compute BCa confidence intervals using boot package. Below is the solution for the plethodon dataset in case if someone wanders into this thread.

Thank you for answering my question!
Kind regards,
Marina

library(geomorph)
library(boot)
library(broom)

data(plethodon)
Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethodon$land)
gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(Y.gpa,
                           site = plethodon$site,
                           species = plethodon$species)

fit_full <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) + site * species, data = gdf,
                     iter = 999, print.progress = FALSE)
gp <- interaction(plethodon$site, plethodon$species)

# disparity
md <- tapply(rowSums(resid(fit_full)^2), gp, mean)

# function to compute md on bootstrapped data
get_md <- function(data, indices, fit, gp){
  Z <- data[indices, ]

form <-fit$LM$form
  gdf2 <- fit$LM$data

gdf2$Y <- Z[, -1]
  gdf2$Csize <- Z[, 1] # non universal (need to change the variable name
                       # to match the name in the data and formula)
  New_fit_full <- procD.lm(form, data = gdf2, iter = 0, print.progress = FALSE)

d2.i <- rowSums(resid(New_fit_full)^2)
  smr <- by(d2.i, gp, mean)
  smr
}

# bootstrap
set.seed(302354)
boot_out <- boot(data = cbind(gdf$Csize, fit_full$LM$Y),
                 statistic = get_md,
                 R = 1000, # increase for final calculation
                 strata = gp, # bootstrap by group
                 fit = fit_full,
                 gp = gp)
# tidy confidence limits with BCa for all groups via broom package
tidy_cl <- tidy(boot_out, conf.int = TRUE, conf.method = "bca")

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data = tidy_cl, aes(x = term, y = statistic)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high))

Marina et al. (Mike, Dean and Antigoni),

To add to both Mike and Dean's point on using (non-parametric) bootstrapping based on empirical resampling to compute confidence intervals.

As mentioned in a couple of the papers/books that Dean mentioned, the "percentile"  based confidence intervals (like Mike calculated) are usually an ok starting point,  but are often problematic for somewhat skewed distributions (of resampled estimates, not raw data),  when the observed estimate is near a boundary (e.g. the observed value is close to the minimum possible value it can take for the data set) and with small within group sample sizes. There are some immediate checks (the boot library can help) and the Bias Corrected and Accelerated CIs (BCa) often can provide an improvement. These problems do occur more often for "variance"/"disparity" and phenotypic integration related statistics in my experience (which makes sense because of both being higher moment statistics that are estimated and also are used bounded by a minimum value, with real estimates sometimes "near" that value).  Like Mike showed in the first example, it is usually most sensible to do the sampling within groups of focus (in the boot library this is done via the strata argument, but it is relatively straightforward to code like Mike showed).

So it pays to take some time and patience to work on this. For the particular data set that Mike showed the example for, things mostly behaved reasonably well. In other situations (see our methods in Haber and Dworkin 2017 in Evolution for some discussion of these issues), things can get a bit bonkers though!

The most robust approach for generating CIs from non parametric bootstrapping (sampling with replacement) is the studentized bootstrap. This has greater computational demands as it requires bootstraps of bootstrap samples (to generate standard errors of each resampled data set to normalize the value we use each iteration). Typically (in my experience) this requires about 200 iterations in the internal resampling, so for a typical "10000" bootstrap iterations, it is really computationally more like 20,000,000 iterations total. Thankfully there are ways of making this more efficient so it still (on a relatively new laptop) will only be on the order of 10-20 minutes to run all these iterations. It can also be parallelized relatively easily in R (with some package dependencies). I keep meaning to write a little add-on set of functions to interact with geomorph/RRPP model objects to do so (I have some working examples just with base R, lm functions not with geomorph). Hopefully (if someone bugs me in the late spring), I can sit down and hammer this out, and send the code to Antigoni, Mike and Dean, or just make a little side package. All the best to all of the morphometrics community, and wishing you all a very happy (Gregorian) new year!

Marina,

I’m happy you were able to solve this.  It looks like your results are superficially similar to the within-group results I previously found, despite different confidence limits summarized.  It should not be a surprise that confidence intervals are asymmetric if the statistic is a variance, which must be positive.  Any “odd” outcomes (e.g., frequent sampling of values that produce large residuals) will be extreme in a positive direction, which will positively skew the distribution of random variances.  I’m willing to bet a log-transformation of the variances will produce symmetric confidence intervals.

Best,

Dear Ian, Mike, Dean and Antigoni,

thank you for great advices! Percentile confidence intervals for my data were indeed very asymmetric. Thanks to your help, I was able to compute BCa confidence intervals using boot package. Below is the solution for the plethodon dataset in case if someone wanders into this thread.

library(geomorph)
library(boot)
library(broom)

data(plethodon)
Y.gpa <- gpagen(plethodon$land)
gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(Y.gpa,
                           site = plethodon$site,
                           species = plethodon$species)

fit_full <- procD.lm(coords ~ log(Csize) + site * species, data = gdf,
                     iter = 999, print.progress = FALSE)
gp <- interaction(plethodon$site, plethodon$species)
# disparity
md <- tapply(rowSums(resid(fit_full)^2), gp, mean)

# function to compute md on bootstrapped data
get_md <- function(data, indices, fit, gp){
  Z <- data[indices, ]
  form <-fit$LM$form
  gdf2 <- fit$LM$data
  gdf2$Y <- Z[, -1]
  gdf2$Csize <- Z[, 1] # non universal (need to change the variable name
                       # to match the name in the data and formula)
  New_fit_full <- procD.lm(form, data = gdf2, iter = 0, print.progress = FALSE)
  d2.i <- rowSums(resid(New_fit_full)^2)
  smr <- by(d2.i, gp, mean)
  smr
}

# bootstrap
set.seed(302354)
boot_out <- boot(data = cbind(gdf$Csize, fit_full$LM$Y),
                 statistic = get_md,
                 R = 1000, # increase for final calculation
                 strata = gp, # bootstrap by group
                 fit = fit_full,
                 gp = gp)
# tidy confidence limits with BCa for all groups via broom package
tidy_cl <- tidy(boot_out, conf.int = TRUE, conf.method = "bca")

library(ggplot2)
ggplot(data = tidy_cl, aes(x = term, y = statistic)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = conf.low, ymax = conf.high))

Marina et al. (Mike, Dean and Antigoni),

To add to both Mike and Dean's point on using (non-parametric) bootstrapping based on empirical resampling to compute confidence intervals.

As mentioned in a couple of the papers/books that Dean mentioned, the "percentile"  based confidence intervals (like Mike calculated) are usually an ok starting point,  but are often problematic for somewhat skewed distributions (of resampled estimates, not raw data),  when the observed estimate is near a boundary (e.g. the observed value is close to the minimum possible value it can take for the data set) and with small within group sample sizes. There are some immediate checks (the boot library can help) and the Bias Corrected and Accelerated CIs (BCa) often can provide an improvement. These problems do occur more often for "variance"/"disparity" and phenotypic integration related statistics in my experience (which makes sense because of both being higher moment statistics that are estimated and also are used bounded by a minimum value, with real estimates sometimes "near" that value).  Like Mike showed in the first example, it is usually most sensible to do the sampling within groups of focus (in the boot library this is done via the strata argument, but it is relatively straightforward to code like Mike showed).

So it pays to take some time and patience to work on this. For the particular data set that Mike showed the example for, things mostly behaved reasonably well. In other situations (see our methods in Haber and Dworkin 2017 in Evolution for some discussion of these issues), things can get a bit bonkers though!

The most robust approach for generating CIs from non parametric bootstrapping (sampling with replacement) is the studentized bootstrap. This has greater computational demands as it requires bootstraps of bootstrap samples (to generate standard errors of each resampled data set to normalize the value we use each iteration). Typically (in my experience) this requires about 200 iterations in the internal resampling, so for a typical "10000" bootstrap iterations, it is really computationally more like 20,000,000 iterations total. Thankfully there are ways of making this more efficient so it still (on a relatively new laptop) will only be on the order of 10-20 minutes to run all these iterations. It can also be parallelized relatively easily in R (with some package dependencies). I keep meaning to write a little add-on set of functions to interact with geomorph/RRPP model objects to do so (I have some working examples just with base R, lm functions not with geomorph). Hopefully (if someone bugs me in the late spring), I can sit down and hammer this out, and send the code to Antigoni, Mike and Dean, or just make a little side package. But, alas no time until at least the end of next semester. But if someone does bug me I will work on it. I keep meaning to, but I keep thinking it is just us who suffers with this.

Hi Marina,

I believe there are several issues you are encountering.  

First, I don’t think you want to bootstrap residuals from the null model.  This seems to attempt to combine the philosophy of a permutation test and bootstrapping confidence intervals for the estimation of variances.

Second, I think you want to resample within groups, not across all values.  Below is an update to your function that allows this.  (Note also it is not necessary to redo the pairwise test step.)

# Function to bootstrap residuals within groups
sample.win.gp <- function(Res, gp) {
  gp.res <- as.list(by(Res, gp, function(x) x)) # separate Res by groups
  ind <- lapply(gpn, function(x) sample(seq_len(x), replace = TRUE)) # sampling frame
  gp.boot <- lapply(1:length(ind), function(j) gp.res[[j]][ind[[j]], ]) # bootstrap within gp levels
  gp.boot <- do.call(rbind, gp.boot) # put back into matrix
  gp.boot <- gp.boot[order(gp), ] # order as original
  gp.boot
}

for(i in 1:999) {
  New_res <- sample.win.gp(Res, gp)
  gdf$New_obs <- Ftt + New_res
  New_fit_full <- procD.lm(New_obs ~ log(Csize) + site * species, 
                           data = gdf, iter = 0, print.progress = FALSE)
  d2.i <- rowSums(resid(New_fit_full)^2)
  smr <- by(d2.i, gp, mean)
  vars <- cbind(vars, smr)
}

# confidence limits
(cl <- apply(vars, 1, quantile, probs = c(0.025, 0.975)))

Third, one could argue that because you have size in your model, bootstrapping should make sure to also match the size and shape of specimens.  This would require using the same sampling frame for bootstrapping observed data and Csize, and refitting the model to obtain residuals.  That is a different algorithm, but an easy one to implement.  In the New_res step within the loop, substituted Res with a concatenated (cbinded) matrix of fit_full$LM$Y and Csize, separate them, and update the data frame; e.g.,

bootstrapped <- sample.win.gp(cbind(gdf$Csize, fit_full$LM$Y, gp)
gdf2 <- gdf
gdf2$New_obs <- bootstrapped[, -1]
gdf$Csize <- bootstarpped[,1]
New_fit_full <- procD.lm(New_obs ~ log(Csize) + site * species, 
                           data = gdf2, iter = 0, print.progress = FALSE)

Doing this will make sure that size and shape match.  I recommend doing this if allometry is important to preserve.

Keep in mind that the confidence limits for estimation and from a permutation test are different things.  The UCL in the pairwise summary is the upper confidence limit of the sampling distribution for a test statistic, not confidence limits around the estimation of the descriptive statistic.  The former is a limit in a statistical test where one would change their opinion to “significant”, based on a null model used to generate random test statistics.  The latter defines the precision of the estimation of the descriptive statistic.  Descriptive and test statistics can be the same thing but the respective distributions are not the same, nor are their expected values based on different resampling schemes.

Hope this helps!
Mike
